text: Validation confirms a system is clean enough to go back online. It doesn't mean every recovered system should go back online at the same moment. Real recovery is phased: systems return in priority order, in small groups, with a deliberate pause between each one to confirm nothing's wrong before the next group is approved to go live.

Meridian grouped its systems into three tiers by business criticality and validation confidence. Tier 1 came back first — domain controllers and core infrastructure the rest of the environment depends on, already fully validated. Tier 2 followed a day later, once Tier 1 showed no trouble: the billing database server and the Gateway itself. Tier 3, general workstations, came back in batches over two more days, not all 200 at once.

Between phases, Meridian's SOC doesn't just wait and hope — it actively watches for the same signals that gave the incident away the first time. The exact account-creation and scheduled-task event IDs from Lesson 17's eradication work get monitored continuously now across every recovered host, not just checked once during cleanup and then forgotten about.

Restoring everything at once feels faster, and under pressure to get revenue-generating systems back online quickly, it's a genuinely tempting shortcut. But validation is a confidence level, not a guarantee — if it missed something on even one system, a full simultaneous restore makes that gap live across the entire environment immediately, with nothing smaller or earlier to catch it first.

Phasing trades a slower recovery for exactly that early warning: a problem surfacing in Tier 1 simply stops Tiers 2 and 3 from going live yet, so the blast radius of a missed validation stays small instead of environment-wide. With the system validated and recovering safely, the incident moves into Chapter 6 — starting with the lessons-learned meeting that turns this response into a better one next time.
